title: The marker with the answer key
allegory: A scorer is like an exam marker holding the answer key: for each finished script it finds the student's answer, compares it with the key, and writes a mark with a note in the margin, and a careless marker can move the class average as much as the students can.

chapters.name: Who marks the script?
chapters.note: the last link in the chain

cap.1: The model has answered a thousand questions. Someone must mark each one against the key, the same way every time, and note why.
cap.2: In Inspect, solvers produce the answer and a scorer grades it. A scorer takes the final TaskState and the sample's target and returns a Score: a value, optionally with the parsed answer and an explanation.
cap.3: The scorer is where the model's text becomes the eval's number. Per-sample Scores are then reduced by metrics such as accuracy, so every aggregate inherits the scorer's parsing choices.

props.label: A B C D: circled B

cap.1: One marker lays a stencil over the multiple-choice boxes: fast and exact. For essays, a second marker reads with a rubric. Both write a mark and a reason.
cap.2: String-matching scorers like match compare the answer with the target: right for MCQs. model_graded_fact asks a model whether the answer contains the target fact, for when a string comparison won't do.
cap.3: Deterministic scorers are cheap and reproducible but brittle to format; model-graded scorers handle paraphrase but inherit judge biases. Choose per task, and log the explanation either way.

parts.note: the mark, the answer found, the reason

cap.1: A marker takes two things, the script and the key, and hands back a mark with a note in the margin. That's the whole job.
cap.2: The exercise writes this function: pull the answer out of state.output, compare it with target, and return a Score. The @scorer decorator also names the metrics, such as accuracy, that summarise it.
cap.3: Scores are per sample; metrics such as accuracy and stderr aggregate them. Keeping the parsed answer and explanation in each Score makes every aggregate traceable to individual transcripts in the log.

chapters.name: The lazy tick
chapters.title: two markers, the same four replies

cap.1: A lazy marker ticks any script where the right letter appears anywhere. 'ANSWER: C' gets a tick when the key is A, because 'ANSWER' contains an A.
cap.2: Parse first, then compare: take the letter after 'ANSWER:', ignore case, and record unreadable replies as no answer rather than wrong. Then read a few transcripts in the log to check the parse.
cap.3: Scorer bugs are silent: a substring check inflates accuracy, a case-sensitive parse deflates it. Count parse failures separately; a sentinel entering the distribution as a judgement is worse than a biased judge.

chapters.name: Tone over truth

right.title: anchored rubric
lines: a confident wrong example scored low

chapters.verdict: A judge grades what it can see, so give it something concrete to compare.

cap.1: An essay marker with no rubric rewards long, confident essays, even wrong ones. Spell out what a 0, a 50 and a 100 look like, and it marks the content.
cap.2: Zheng et al. (2023) found GPT-4 judges agree with humans over 80% of the time, but named position, verbosity and self-enhancement bias. Anchor the scale, give examples, and ask for the reason before the score.
cap.3: Model-graded scorers need measurement discipline: anchored endpoints, few-shot examples with a confident wrong answer scored low, the explanation before the integer, parse failures counted, extremes read by hand.

cap.1: Every claim about what an AI can or will do rests on a marker. If the marker is sloppy, you steer by a number that measures the marking, not the model.
cap.2: Scorers decide what every eval number means, from MCQ benchmarks to the AI control monitor, a model-graded scorer rating suspiciousness. Read one sample's full log before believing the score.
cap.3: Scores can carry metadata, which is how ARENA's control notebook keeps the clean-or-backdoored label beside each suspiciousness score. Measurement validity lives in the scorer, not in the metric.

caption.1: Same 20 replies, same model. Flip how the marker reads them and the score swings from 55% to 85%. Only one setting finds the true 70%.
caption.2: The substring check ticks 'ANSWER: C' when the key is A; a case-sensitive parse misses 'answer: b'. Parse the letter after 'ANSWER:', ignore case, and track replies you couldn't parse.
caption.3: Scorer choice alone moves this metric by 30 points, in both directions. Validate a scorer on labelled edge cases before trusting any comparison between models built on it.

hamming.what: The function that reads a model's final answer, compares it with the target, and returns a graded Score that metrics like accuracy then aggregate.
hamming.when: Every eval run, as the last step after the solvers: string matching for MCQs, a model judge where a string comparison won't do.
hamming.why: The scorer decides what the eval's number means; a sloppy one measures formatting or tone instead of the property.

object.title: The tilting marking table
object.subtitle: a toy judge: how right, how confident, and the mark it gives

knobs.label: how anchored the rubric is (0 none, 1 fully)

cap.1: A marker with no rubric. Floor: how right the answer is, and how long and confident it sounds. Height is the mark. The slope runs mostly towards confidence.
cap.2: A toy of an unanchored 0-100 judge: with nothing concrete to compare against, it grades what it can see, like length and assertiveness. Zheng et al. measured the length version as verbosity bias.
cap.3: Toy model: mark = 100(0.3·correct + 0.7·confident) when unanchored. The real finding: strong judges agree with humans over 80% of the time, yet show position, verbosity and self-enhancement bias.

cap.1: Compare the two pins. The confident wrong answer sits higher than the hedged right one. This marker is scoring tone, not truth.
cap.2: This is the classic symptom: hand the grader a cautious correct answer and a confident wrong one, and the wrong one scores higher.
cap.3: Confidence and hedging correlate with quality in a judge's training data, so an unanchored judge scores register. Asking for the number before the reason makes it worse.

cap.1: Add a rubric: say what a 0, a 50 and a 100 look like, with examples. The table tilts towards correctness.
cap.2: Anchored endpoints plus few-shot examples, including a confident wrong answer scored low, give the judge something concrete to compare, so less of the mark comes from surface features.
cap.3: Anchoring moves weight from style features to the property. In practice you check it the same way: spot-check the top and bottom of the score distribution by hand.

cap.1: Fully anchored, the mark depends on correctness alone. Then read the highest and lowest marks yourself to check you agree.
cap.2: Reason before number, delimiters the parser can find, parse failures counted apart, and the extremes read by hand. If you disagree with the extremes, fix the rubric.
cap.3: Anchoring is necessary, not sufficient: swap presentation order to average out position bias, avoid self-grading, and use reference-guided grading where the judge must verify.

predict.q: With no rubric, which answer does this marker score higher?
predict.why: Unanchored, it grades what it can see: length and assertiveness. Tone wins over truth.

predict.q: What should come first in the judge's reply?
predict.why: A score produced first is a snap judgement the explanation then rationalises.

predict.q: The judge's reply has no readable score. What do you record?
predict.why: A made-up value entering the distribution as if it were a judgement is worse than a biased judgement.
